talks.title: SEC-T 0x11: Erkan Ekici & Shanti Lindström - Offensive SIEM: When the Blue Team Switches Perspective
talks.teaser: Explores SEC-T 0x11: Erkan Ekici & Shanti Lindström - Offensive SIEM: When the Blue Team Switches Perspective and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that blue teams can turn the logs they already collect into an offensive hunting tool. Using Sysmon and Windows event logs in a central SIEM, the speakers search an entire enterprise for Windows privilege escalation paths instead of inspecting one machine at a time. Their scope covers system services, scheduled tasks, DLL hijacking and failed software deployments, each hunted for programs or files sitting in user-writable locations or behind weak permissions.

For services and scheduled tasks, the queries flag creation events that point to folders such as ProgramData, Users or Windows Temp, along with unquoted service paths. For DLL hijacking, Sysmon image-load events reveal system processes loading DLLs from user-writable folders. One hit involved a print spooler component loading a DLL from a writable Epson printer directory, which the speakers demonstrated as code execution as SYSTEM. In the software deployment case, a SYSTEM process launched from ProgramData led to a folder writable by built-in users, where Process Monitor showed missing DLL lookups that could be planted. A bonus case covered a Windows SDK service under the C: root that gave authenticated users modify rights.

The main takeaway is to treat the SIEM as a vulnerability scanner: tune the queries, turn them into alerts, and then check file and folder permissions on every hit. The speakers said the same approach works with an EDR platform, and they shared their queries in a public repository. Some further findings were withheld while vendor disclosure was pending.

talks.title: SEC-T 0x11: Jonathan Elkabas - Breaking Entra: Real-World Cloud Identity Attacks You Can Recreate
talks.teaser: Analyzes SEC-T 0x11: Jonathan Elkabas - Breaking Entra: Real-World Cloud Identity Attacks You Can Recreate and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary: Jonathan Elkabas introduces EntraGoat, a deliberately vulnerable Microsoft Entra ID lab mirroring attack paths like service-principal ownership abuse, certificate-based app role assignment, group-owned Application Administrator roles, and CBA upload chains. Each scenario ships hints, cleanup scripts, and blog walkthroughs so defenders practice OAuth consent, PIM activation, and administrative unit boundaries without touching production tenants. Elkabas stresses nonhuman identity sprawl statistics from Microsoft and invites testers to run the open CTF only in disposable tenants. Attendees leave with checklists for consent phishing, app registration hygiene, and detecting risky API permissions before adversaries chain them into tenant-wide compromise.

talks.title: SEC-T 0x11: Dan Tentler - How to bug hotel rooms v2.0
talks.teaser: Presents SEC-T 0x11: Dan Tentler - How to bug hotel rooms v2.0 and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how cheap, connected sensors can be used to monitor a hotel room, and why a traveler might want to. The speaker recaps why hotel rooms feel less safe than before, citing impostor security staff and opportunistic theft, and explains that his earlier version relied on cheap peer-to-peer cameras that were easy to find and unreliable. The newer approach uses Home Assistant, an open-source automation platform, as the hub that ties everything together.

The middle of the talk walks through the hardware. A travel router sends traffic over WireGuard to a home network, a Raspberry Pi runs Home Assistant, and Z-Wave and Bluetooth add more sensors. The standout parts are millimeter-wave radar sensors that can detect people through fiberglass or wood doors and count occupants in an adjoining room. CO2 and light readings can also suggest occupancy and activity. A camera can be triggered by a door-open event and push still images to a phone within seconds, so evidence survives even if the camera is taken. The speaker also described picking up nearby Bluetooth devices, such as a toothbrush, at a conference.

The closing section covers the limits. The full kit costs roughly two thousand dollars, and a large battery can keep the sensors running for a few days. Radar and radio emissions are easy for others to detect, so the setup is not covert. Legal status varies by country and state, and the speaker notes that the law has not caught up with this kind of sensing.

talks.title: SEC-T 0x11: Yousif Hussin - Inside Google's Discovery & Remediation of a Critical CPU Vulnerability
talks.teaser: Examines SEC-T 0x11: Yousif Hussin - Inside Googles Discovery & Remediation of a Critical CPU Vulnerability and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary: Yousif Hussein recounts leading Google's cross-team response to Repar, an Intel FSRM microarchitectural bug reachable from cloud tenants and client Chrome OS devices. He frames the incident with assembly primers, explains impact on Borg-managed fleets, and details hot-loading microcode to avoid rebooting production while debating the costly chicken-bit mitigation. The narrative covers embargo coordination, IceBreaker false positives, and automating future CPU responses after measuring attacker-scale VM escape risk. Lessons emphasize inventorying CPU stepping exposure, rehearsing staged rollouts, and treating hypervisor sandboxes as first-class blast-radius calculators rather than afterthought dashboards.

talks.title: SEC-T 0x11: noraj
talks.teaser: Explores SEC-T 0x11: noraj and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at SEC-T 0x11, Alexander (noraj), a pentester at Synactive and maintainer of BlackArch Linux, explores the security risks arising from Unicode's complexity and developers' lack of awareness. Because Unicode unifies older encoding standards and expands to millions of characters through mechanisms like code points, composition, and joining, naive implementations in software frequently lead to vulnerabilities.

### Key Topics
- **Unicode Fundamentals**: Code points (represented standardly as `U+<hex>`), variable-length encodings such as UTF-8 (1 to 4 bytes), composing characters (e.g., combining diacritics), and joining characters (e.g., combining emojis or variation selectors).
- **Visual and Source Code Attacks**: The use of homoglyphs and invisible control characters for phishing, typo-squatting, and backdoor insertion in source code.
- **String Length and Sizing Pitfalls**: Discrepancies between human-visible graphemes, Unicode code points/units, and raw byte lengths across encodings like UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32.
- **Case Transformation Collisions**: Non-bijective casing behavior leading to string length changes, domain collisions, and account takeovers.
- **Normalization Vulnerabilities**: Exploitation of Unicode normalization forms (NFD, NFC, NFKD, NFKC) to execute host splitting and bypass XSS sanitization.

### Technical Details
- **Source Code Backdoors via Homoglyphs & Invisible Characters**: Alexander demonstrates substituting standard syntax operators with homoglyphs, such as replacing an exclamation mark (`!`) in JavaScript with a retroflex click character in a variable name, turning an equality check into a perpetual assignment (`true`). Invisible characters, like the Hangul filler inserted into a JavaScript equality check, can silently trigger unintended code evaluation without visual indication.
- **Sizing Inconsistencies**: A single visible emoji composed of a woman, a joiner, a heart, a color variation selector, another joiner, and a man constitutes one grapheme but six code units, translating into differing byte counts across UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32. Naive length queries in environments like Node.js can return surrogate-pair counts instead of grapheme counts, risking buffer overflows, string truncation, and misaligned sanitization indices.
- **Case Transformation Exploits**: Uppercasing characters like the German Eszett (`ß`) expands one character into two (`SS`), while lowercasing the Kelvin sign (`K`) collapses it to a standard ASCII `k`. In an illustrated password reset flow, an attacker submits `synactive.com` containing the Kelvin sign. The application normalizes the input to lower case for database lookup (retrieving the legitimate admin's account), but dispatches the reset token using the un-lowercased email input, routing the reset email to an attacker-controlled domain.
- **Host Splitting & XSS Filter Bypasses via Normalization**: In compatibility normalization modes (NFKD/NFKC), specific multi-character mappings—such as the "addressed to the subject" glyph normalizing to `a/s`—can split hostnames and turn what appeared to be a subdomain whitelist match (`synactive.<glyph>.target.com`) into an entirely different path and domain. Similarly, passing Unicode characters that transform into `<` or `>` under NFKC/NFKD after an HTML escape function has run allows filters to be bypassed. Alexander also illustrates how NFC recomposition can absorb closing delimiters into attribute values, triggering context breakouts.

### Takeaways
Developers must recognize that Unicode operations—including casing, length measurement, and normalization—can mutate strings in non-trivial ways. Order of operations is critical: data normalization must always occur prior to escaping or validation to prevent mutated payloads from reintroducing dangerous syntax.
